raw_response:
# C03 — catalogue-first references

I found six partial references worth considering. They help with specific mechanisms; this search did not establish an existing design that satisfies every required boundary. Availability by the 2019-04-16 cutoff is unverified unless explicitly stated below.

1. **[kubectl-nsenter](https://github.com/towolf/kubectl-nsenter)** — Its container-to-PID lookup, namespace entry and rootfs access code can inform node-agent attachment mechanics. The [opened implementation](https://github.com/towolf/kubectl-nsenter/blob/master/kubectl-nsenter) requires SSH and runtime-specific host details, so it needs adaptation behind the authorized node-agent/CRI path. Date: unknown. Discovered through [awesome-kubectl-plugins](https://github.com/ishantanu/awesome-kubectl-plugins).

2. **[netshoot](https://github.com/nicolaka/netshoot)** — A separate toolbox image sharing the target's network namespace supplies tools without changing the application image. Filesystem/PID access, admission and API auditing remain separate concerns. The current Kubernetes examples use native debugging and do not prove historical availability. Date: unknown. Discovered through [awesome-k8s-tools](https://github.com/vilaca/awesome-k8s-tools/blob/main/data/repos).

3. **[OPA Gatekeeper](https://github.com/open-policy-agent/gatekeeper)** — Object-based admission can guide checks over a complete requested debug specification. Its [input documentation](https://open-policy-agent.github.io/gatekeeper/website/docs/input/) distinguishes requested and old objects and request context. The debug API still must expose every relevant field and invoke admission; Gatekeeper's resource audit is not an API activity log. Date: unknown; consulted documentation is v3.23.x. Discovered through [awesome-k8s-tools](https://github.com/vilaca/awesome-k8s-tools/blob/main/data/repos).

4. **[containerd CRI plugin](https://github.com/containerd/containerd)** — Its runtime integration and validation references offer a concrete CRI implementation against which debugging-container lifecycle behavior could be designed and checked. The opened source does not verify target-namespace sharing or reduced-capability negotiation. Date: unknown; the README's version statement was not tied to an opened dated release. Discovered through [awesome-k8s-tools](https://github.com/vilaca/awesome-k8s-tools/blob/main/data/repos).

5. **[kubectl-trace](https://github.com/iovisor/kubectl-trace)** — API-visible tracing pods and target-process selection provide an alternative diagnostic-workload model. Its root-namespace and privileged execution requirements make it unsuitable as the complete attachment design. Temporal status: consulted revision contains a 2021-08-10 build example and is treated as post-cutoff evidence; original feature dates remain unverified. Discovered through [awesome-kubectl-plugins](https://github.com/ishantanu/awesome-kubectl-plugins).

6. **[Azure Sidecar pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sidecar)** — A separate helper container offers a packaging and isolation model for debugging tools. Its ordinary shared lifecycle does not supply troubleshooting-time insertion, CRI semantics or admission/audit handling. Temporal status: page last updated 2026-09-01, after cutoff. Discovered through the [Azure pattern catalogue](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns?trk=public_post_comment-text).

The translation suggested by these references is to keep tool packaging separate from attachment mechanics, place the complete debug request in an inspectable API object, and make runtime-specific attachment capabilities explicit. This is my synthesis, not a claim that any listed project already implements that combination or has proved useful for this design.

I excluded the opened aylei/kubectl-debug and ksniff READMEs after encountering proposal-related references. I also conservatively excluded CRI-O's README because its design-proposal link was not verified. None of those proposal links was opened. The current netshoot page exposed native Kubernetes debug usage; that exposure is recorded and its toolbox mechanism is retained only as undated evidence. A catalogue raw-file request was blocked. No retained candidate has verified pre-cutoff availability, and no retained reference establishes the whole required API/node-agent design.

This was an internal separate-context run using GPT-6 Astra Pro, not a human study or a different-model comparison. Gold and other runs were not read.

The current netshoot README includes native Kubernetes debug usage, recorded as exposure; its retained mechanism is undated rather than claimed pre-cutoff.
No retained candidate has verified availability by the cutoff. Unknown dates with post_decision=false must not be interpreted as evidence of pre-cutoff availability.
kubectl-trace's consulted revision contains a 2021 build example; the original dates of its individual capabilities remain unverified.
The raw awesome-docker README request was blocked. It was not retried through an alternate route.

None of the retained references was shown to satisfy all boundaries; especially missing is a verified complete API/node-agent design combining full-spec admission, activity auditing, filesystem attachment and portable runtime capability handling.
No software was installed, executed or deployed; usefulness here is a proposed transfer, not a demonstrated outcome.
